userPrompt: Can I require employees to work more than 48 hours a week in the EU?
responseText:
**No, not as a blanket requirement.**

In the EU, the **Working Time Directive (2003/88/EC)** applies across all Member States and sets a hard limit:

- **Maximum average working time**: 48 hours per week, **including overtime**, averaged over a reference period (usually 4 months, but up to 6 or 12 months in some countries).
- This is a **mandatory** rule. You cannot impose a contract or policy that requires employees to work more than 48 hours per week on average.

### Key points for employers:
- Employees have the **right to refuse** to work beyond 48 hours. You cannot discipline, dismiss, or disadvantage them for it.
- **Opt-out agreements** are allowed in most (but not all) Member States. An individual employee can voluntarily opt out in writing, but:
  - It must be genuinely voluntary.
  - It can usually be withdrawn with notice (typically 1–3 months).
  - Some countries (e.g. France, Spain, Netherlands) heavily restrict or discourage opt-outs.
- Certain sectors or roles (e.g. executives, doctors in training in some countries) may have exceptions or different rules, but these are narrow.
- Night work, rest periods (11 consecutive hours per day, 24/48 hours weekly), and annual leave rules still apply on top.

### Practical reality:
Most EU employers cannot lawfully require more than 48 hours/week as a condition of employment. Systematic excess hours usually require individual opt-outs + proper recording of hours. Many countries (Germany, France, Belgium, Italy, etc.) also have stricter national laws or collective agreements that cap hours even lower or add extra safeguards.

**Recommendation**: Consult the specific rules of the Member State(s) where the employees work. National implementation and enforcement vary significantly. In some countries, labour inspectorates or courts treat excessive hours very seriously (fines, back pay, criminal liability in extreme cases).
